solar-system-explorer: Choose your date of birth and type your weight on Earth in kilograms or pounds. The table fills in straight away.
See how old you are in each planet's years, the date of your next birthday there, and what the scales would show on each planet.
Pick any two bodies, from the Sun to the Moon, to see them drawn to the same scale and how many times wider one is.
Scroll to the planets drawn side by side and the fact table for day length, year length, gravity, distance and moons.
learn-the-clock: Drag the short red hand to change the hour and the long blue hand to change the minutes. When the long hand goes past 12, the short hand moves on, just like a real clock.
Look at the clock and say the time out loud. Then tap "Tap to see the time" to check the numbers and the words, such as "half past three".
Pick a level, from o'clock up to every minute. Read the clock and choose the time, or set the hands to the time you are given. A round has 10 questions.
Make a printable sheet of 12 clocks. Draw the hands for each time, or write the time shown. Print it without answers for the child and with answers to mark it.
kids-maths-practice: Pick adding, taking away, times tables, sharing (dividing), money in rupees, or a bit of everything. Then choose Easy, Medium or Hard.
Answer 10 questions one at a time. Type the answer and press Check. You see right away whether it is correct, with the answer, and a score at the end.
Open the Worksheet tab for a sheet of 20 different problems (10 for money word problems). Press New worksheet for another set.
Switch on Show the answers to mark the sheet. Switch it off again before you print the copy for the child.

explainersSolarSystem.title: Solar System Explorer
explainersSolarSystem.subtitle: See your age and weight on every planet, compare any two worlds in size, and view the planets to scale with their key facts. Free, no sign-up.
faq: How is my age on another planet worked out?

A planet's year is the time it takes to go once round the Sun. The tool counts the days since you were born and divides them by that planet's year in Earth days, for example 88 days for Mercury and about 687 for Mars. Mercury's short year makes you look much older there, and Neptune's year of about 165 Earth years means most people have not yet had a first birthday.
Why does my weight change but not my mass?

Mass is the amount of matter in your body and it never changes. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass. Mars pulls about 38 percent as hard as Earth, so a person who weighs 60 kg on Earth would read about 23 kg on a scale there, while Jupiter's pull is more than twice Earth's. The tool multiplies your Earth weight by the planet's surface gravity and divides by Earth's.
Jupiter and Saturn have no ground. What does surface gravity mean there?

For the gas giants, the surface is taken as the level in the atmosphere where the pressure equals Earth's sea-level pressure, roughly the cloud tops. You could not stand on it, so the weight shown is what a scale would read if you could float at that level.
Is a day on Venus really longer than its year?

Yes. Venus turns very slowly, taking about 243 Earth days to spin once on its axis, and it goes round the Sun in about 225 Earth days. It also spins backwards compared with most planets, so the Sun would rise in the west.
Where do the numbers come from, and how accurate are they?

The figures are rounded from the NASA planetary fact sheets, which are public. Sizes, distances and gravity are averages, because planets are not perfect spheres and orbits are not perfect circles. The number of moons keeps growing as astronomers find new ones, so those entries are shown with a plus sign.
Is my date of birth or weight uploaded?
No. Everything is worked out in your browser and nothing you type is sent to {{siteName}}. The page still loads advertising and other resources from the network.

explainersLearnClock.title: Learn the Clock
explainersLearnClock.subtitle: A friendly analog clock for kids. Move the hands by touch, check the time in words, take a quiz with levels, and print clock worksheets. Free, private, no sign-up.
faq: At what age can children learn to tell time?

Most children begin to read o'clock times around age 5 or 6 and can usually read to the quarter hour and five minutes by age 7 or 8. Every child is different, so go at the pace that feels comfortable. The levels here start with whole hours and move up to every minute.
In what order should a child learn the clock?

A common order is: hour hand and the numbers, o'clock, half past, quarter past and quarter to, then five-minute steps, then single minutes. The quiz levels follow this order, so you can start at the first level and move on when the answers come easily.
Why are the two hands different colours and lengths?

The short red hand shows the hour and the long blue hand shows the minutes. Mixing them up is the most common mistake, so the colours and the lengths give two clues. In the quiz, one of the wrong answers is the time you would get if the two hands were swapped.
Why does the short hand move when I move the long hand?

On a real clock the hour hand creeps forward as the minutes pass, so at half past three it sits halfway between the 3 and the 4. The clock here does the same, which shows children why the hour hand is not always exactly on a number.
What do "half past", "quarter past" and "quarter to" mean?

"Half past" means 30 minutes after the hour, with the long hand on the 6. "Quarter past" means 15 minutes after, with the long hand on the 3. "Quarter to" means 15 minutes before the next hour, with the long hand on the 9.
Can I print the worksheets?

Yes. Choose a level and a kind of worksheet, press New worksheet for a different set, and print or save as a PDF. You can show the answers to mark the sheet, then hide them and print a clean copy for the child.
Does it work on a phone or tablet?
Yes. The hands can be moved with a finger, a mouse or a pen. If dragging is hard, there are buttons under the clock that move the hour and the minutes one step at a time.
Is anything stored or uploaded?
No. The clock, the quiz and the worksheets all run in your browser, and nothing is sent to {{siteName}}. Scores are not saved.

explainersKidsMaths.title: Kids Maths Practice
explainersKidsMaths.subtitle: Maths practice for young children: adding, taking away, times tables, dividing and rupee word problems. A 10-question quiz and printable worksheets with answers. Free, private, no sign-up.
faq: Which classes is this for?

The Easy level suits children in classes 1 and 2: adding and taking away within 20, and the tables of 2, 5 and 10. Medium suits classes 2 and 3 with numbers to 100 and tables to 10. Hard goes to numbers to 1000 and tables to 12, for classes 3 and 4. Use the level that feels a little challenging but not stressful.
What kind of money problems are there?

Word problems in rupees like the ones in school books: finding the price of one thing from another, the total of two things, how much two children have together, how much is left after buying several items, and how much change to get back. The prices are round numbers, so the sums are about the maths and not the coins.
Do the questions repeat?
Each quiz and worksheet is made fresh from random numbers, so there is always something new to practise. The 20 problems on a worksheet are all different from each other.
Why type the answer instead of choosing from options?
Typing makes children work the answer out instead of guessing, which is better practice. The keyboard shown on a phone or tablet is the number pad.
How do I print a worksheet for my child?

Open the Worksheet tab, choose the topic and level, press New worksheet if you like, make sure Show the answers is off, and press Print or save as PDF. For your own marking copy, switch the answers on and print again.
Can this replace schoolwork?
No. It is for extra practice at home or in class. If a child finds a level very hard or too easy, move up or down a level and come back to it later.
Is my child's score saved?
No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing is sent to {{siteName}} or stored. The score only shows during the round.

sections.heading: Why a planet's year changes your age
paragraphs: We measure age in Earth years because Earth takes about 365 days to circle the Sun. A planet closer to the Sun has less distance to travel and moves faster, so its year is shorter. Mercury finishes an orbit in 88 days, which means a 30-year-old has lived through about 124 Mercury years.

Far from the Sun the opposite happens. Jupiter takes almost 12 Earth years to go round once, Saturn about 29 and Neptune about 165. Nobody has lived long enough to see a full Neptune year, so the tool shows your age there as a small decimal.

sections.heading: Mass, weight and gravity
paragraphs: Gravity grows with the mass of a planet and falls as you move away from its centre, so a big planet with a wide body can still pull less than you would expect. Saturn is nearly ten times heavier than Earth in mass but spreads that mass over a huge, light body, so its cloud tops pull only slightly less than Earth's surface.

On the Moon, gravity is about one sixth of Earth's, which is why astronauts could take long, slow bounding steps. On the Sun, a surface pull of 274 m/s squared would make a 60 kg person weigh as much as a small truck.

sections.heading: Reading the size comparison
paragraphs: Both circles in the comparison use the same scale, so you can judge the real difference in width. Jupiter is about eleven times wider than Earth, yet more than a thousand Earths would fit inside it by volume, because volume grows with the cube of the width.
The planet line-up shows how small the rocky planets are next to the gas and ice giants. Mercury is barely a dot beside Jupiter.

sections.heading: Why the clock is hard to learn
paragraphs: An analog clock asks a child to read two hands at once, count in fives, and understand that the same face is used for hours and minutes. It is no surprise that this takes practice. Moving the hands themselves, not just looking at them, helps children see how the hour hand and the minute hand are connected.
Try to keep sessions short, five or ten minutes, and finish on a question the child got right.

sections.heading: A simple way to teach it
paragraphs: Start with the short hand and the numbers. Ask the child to set the clock to 3 o'clock, then 7 o'clock, and notice that the long hand always points straight up. Move on to half past, where the long hand points down to the 6, then to quarter past and quarter to.
When those feel easy, count in fives round the clock face, which links each number to its minute count: the 1 means 5 minutes, the 2 means 10 minutes, and so on. Only then move to single minutes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
paragraphs: Reading the two hands the wrong way round is the most frequent mistake, so name them out loud: short hand for hours, long hand for minutes. Another is saying the wrong hour for times after half past. At 3:45 the short hand is almost at the 4, and we say "quarter to four". Moving the minute hand slowly past the top of the clock here shows how the hour hand moves on.

sections.heading: Using the quiz and worksheets
paragraphs: The Read the clock quiz shows a clock and four times to choose from, and the wrong answers are the ones children really pick, such as the hour one too high or the hands swapped. Set the clock turns it round: a time is given and the child moves the hands. The worksheets give offline practice, and the answer key lets a parent or teacher mark them quickly.

sections.heading: Little and often works best
paragraphs: Five to ten minutes of maths a day does more than one long session a week. A 10-question round takes about that long. Stop on a correct answer so that the child ends feeling successful.
If your child gets most answers right, move up a level. If they get fewer than half right, move down and come back later. The goal is steady, relaxed progress.

sections.heading: Learning the tables
paragraphs: Start with the tables of 2, 5 and 10, which have clear patterns, then 3 and 4, then the harder ones. Practise a single table until it is easy before mixing them. The Sharing option works the same facts backwards: 35 divided by 5 is 7 because 5 times 7 is 35. Seeing both together makes the tables stick.

sections.heading: Money word problems
paragraphs: Word problems are where children learn to decide what to do with the numbers. Ask them to read the question twice and say in their own words what is being asked: do we add, take away, or share? Underlining the numbers and the key words, such as "more than", "in all" and "left", helps.
Counting real coins and notes while solving a problem, or playing shop at home, brings the same idea to life.

sections.heading: Using the worksheets
paragraphs: Printed sheets give children a break from the screen and let them show their working. Ask them to write the working in the margin for the harder sums. Use the answer key to mark the sheet together, and talk about the mistakes, not only the score.
